## Versailles and The French Revolution 1789 - 1803
Revolutionary poster.
© Château de Versailles, Dist. RMN / © Christophe Fouin
Le lien vers le site collection
Far from having been pillaged by a rampant mob as might be imagined, the Palace of Versailles came through the period of the French Revolution relatively unscathed, even though some would not have minded seeing such a key symbol of the monarchical system laid to waste.
Find out more about Versailles and the French Revolution
The King’s Buildings service took advantage of the departure of the royal family for the Tuileries on 6 October 1789 to begin repairs that would have been rather awkward to carry out in the presence of the Court, such as restoring the ceiling paintings in the Hall of Mirrors. The fall of the monarchy in August 1792 ushered in a period of uncertainty, even though the Convention had decreed that the maintenance of the former royal residences devolved to the nation.
Both during and for some time after this period, there was a question over the use of areas that had been partly appropriated, usually on a temporary basis, for other uses such as arms manufacturing, which went on in the South Wing before moving to the Grand Commun buildings.
Nevertheless, two decisions that were to have significant consequences for the palace were taken just after the fall of the Ancien Régime.
In August 1793, the Central Museum for the Arts opened in Paris, to the detriment of Versailles. The initial stock comprised collections of paintings and sculptures belonging to the Crown, while works that had decorated the State Apartments or that had been kept in the stores of the "Surintendance des Bâtiments" were transferred to the Louvre. The sculptures that decorated the Gardens of Versailles were not involved in the move, however. Objections raised by the municipality and the Department only served to slow the process down but were unable to prevent the removal of masterpieces that had featured in all guides of Versailles published before the French Revolution.

## Versailles and The French Revolution 1789 - 1803
In another development, a law passed on 10 June 1793 stipulated the disposal of all the contents of the former palaces of the Crown, apart from “works of art and science”. All of the furniture and furnishings concerned that had not accompanied the royal family to the Tuileries or had not been sent to the Furniture Store-House or requisitioned for various services were sold off over the course of almost a year, between 25 August 1793 and 11 August 1794. No fewer than 17,182 lots were on offer, the vast majority of which were acquired by Paris merchants and “citizens”.
Painted by Hubert Robert in the late 18 th century, this painting depicts the installation of the central nave where a statue of Isis was set up. This statue was removed from Versailles during the French Revolution as it was part of Louis XIV's private collections.
©Château de Versailles, Dist. RMN / © Christophe Fouin
Le lien vers le site collection
Although the furniture and many of the works of art had been removed, the palace continued to be an attraction, with guided tours still being organised. In any case, it was not totally deserted because in 1793 it was designated as a Public Repository, i.e. a place for storing and sorting all items confiscated in the Department of Seine et Oise, whether from migrants, convicts or religious institutions. It was on the basis of these seizures and whatever had not yet left the palace that the project was launched in 1794 to establish a museum, which, after a somewhat chaotic installation period, opened in 1796.
A science room covering natural history and physical sciences was set up on the ground floor of the North Wing, while a library was established on the ground floor of the South Wing. The State Apartments and the Queen's Apartments were used to display paintings, as well as vases and other collectibles, which were placed on marble tables.
texts.7:
## Versailles and The French Revolution 1789 - 1803
This last section underwent considerable change, becoming, in 1797, the Special Museum of the French School. Dedicated solely to French painters past and present, it entailed a further exchange of works between the Paris museums and Versailles, with the latter having to relinquish paintings and antiques it still held from foreign schools in return for paintings and sculptures by French artists. This short-lived museum, which opened in 1801 only to close its doors again in 1803, helped make the connection between the paintings hanging on the walls and the painted ceilings in the apartments.
Other areas were also given over to the arts as, at the same time, the Comédie-Française took over Marie-Antoinette’s former theatre, featuring designs by Hubert Robert, in the Gabriel Wing.

## Discover the Waterfalls of Iceland
Iceland is home to thousands of waterfalls, shaped by glaciers, rivers, and dramatic volcanic landscapes. One of the best-known in North Iceland is Goðafoss. Photo: Ragnar Th. Sigurdsson / Arctic Images
There are waterfalls, and then there are Iceland’s waterfalls. Some drop into deep canyons, others flow over ancient lava, and a few even let you walk behind the falling water. With glaciers, frequent rains, volcanic landscapes, and plenty of dramatic changes in elevation, Iceland has just the right ingredients for waterfalls. And there are a lot of them.
Planning a trip to Iceland? Here are some of the most popular and impressive waterfalls in Iceland, region by region. Plus, practical information to help you visit them safely.

## Map of Iceland’s Most Popular Waterfalls
Iceland’s waterfalls are scattered right around the country. So, there’s a good chance you’ll encounter several without making much of a detour. Many sit close to Iceland’s Ring Road (Route 1), while others require a short walk or a proper hike.
Use the map to get your bearings, then explore the regions below to find waterfalls that fit naturally into your route.

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
Several of the country’s best-known waterfalls are in South Iceland. This makes them easy additions to the Golden Circle or a South Coast road trip.

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
### 1. Gullfoss
There’s a reason Gullfoss is one of Iceland’s most famous natural sights. The Hvítá River rushes over two stages before disappearing into a rugged canyon, sending spray high above the falls. Its name means “Golden Falls.” And that’s where the Golden Circle route got its name, featuring Gullfoss, the Geysir Geothermal Area, and Þingvellir National Park.
Several viewing areas let you experience this beautiful waterfall from different angles. Depending on the Icelandic weather, you might get sunshine and rainbows, moody mist, or a snow-covered winter landscape. Gullfoss handles all three rather well.
**Practical information about Gullfoss Waterfall:**
*   **Location:** Golden Circle, South Iceland  
*   **Access:** Easy; short paths lead from the parking area to viewing platforms  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Yes, although individual paths may close when conditions are icy  
*   **Good to know:** The upper walkway gives you a panoramic view, while the lower path brings you closer to the rushing water

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
### 2. Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi
What makes Seljalandsfoss special is the chance to walk behind the waterfall. A path curves behind its tall curtain of water, giving you a unique perspective of the South Coast landscape.
Keep walking, and you’ll reach the nearby Gljúfrabúi. It’s partly concealed inside a narrow gorge and feels completely different despite being only a short distance away. Reaching the best view involves stepping into the opening of the gorge, so waterproof shoes are a very good idea.
**Practical information about Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi waterfalls**
*   **Location:** South Coast, just off the Ring Road  
*   **Access:** Seljalandsfoss is a short walk from the parking area; Gljúfrabúi is a few minutes farther on foot  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Yes, conditions permitting; paths can become icy  
*   **Good to know:** The path behind Seljalandsfoss may close when ice makes it unsafe
At Seljalandsfoss, visitors can follow the path behind the waterfall and experience the South Coast scenery from a different perspective. Photo: Ragnar Th. Sigurdsson/ Arctic Images

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
### 3. Skógafoss & Kvernufoss
Skógafoss is one of South Iceland's most recognizable waterfalls. The broad waterfall drops about 60 metres (197 feet) from the region's former sea cliffs. When it is sunny, the spray often creates colourful rainbows.
You can admire it from below or climb the staircase beside the falls for a higher viewpoint. Nearby, Kvernufoss offers a different experience. A short walk leads into a gorge where, in suitable conditions, a path also curves behind the waterfall.
**Practical information about Skógafoss & Kvernufoss waterfalls:**
*   **Location:** Near Skógar, South Iceland  
*   **Access:** Skógafoss is beside the parking area; Kvernufoss requires a short walk  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Generally, yes, but snow and ice can affect trails and steps  
*   **Good to know:** If you climb the stairs at Skógafoss, the trail continues into the Highlands past many more waterfalls

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
### 4. Svartifoss
Dark basalt columns surround Svartifoss as it drops through the Skaftafell landscape. These distinctive rock formations also inspired the design of Hallgrímskirkja Church in Reykjavík.
Svartifoss lies in Skaftafell, part of Vatnajökull National Park. And unlike the roadside giants of the South Coast, you’ll need to stretch your legs to see it. Maintained trails, particularly S2-Svartifoss, lead through the Skaftafell landscape to the falls.
**Practical information about Svartifoss Waterfall:**
*   **Location:** Skaftafell, Vatnajökull National Park  
*   **Access:** A 3-kilometre (1.9-mile) out-and-back hike required from the parking area  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Potentially, but trail conditions vary with snow and ice  
*   **Good to know:** The trail to the site passes a few smaller waterfalls like Hundafoss and Magnúsarfoss
A cinematic moment at Háifoss in South Iceland, featured in the final season of Stranger Things. © Netflix

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
### 5. Háifoss
Háifoss means “High Waterfall,” and at around 122 m (400 ft), it certainly lives up to its name. The Fossá River plunges into a deep canyon in Þjórsárdalur, with neighbouring Granni adding another waterfall to the scene.
_Stranger Things_ fans might recognise this landscape, too. Háifoss and Granni made an appearance in the show’s final season, giving you one more reason to visit it. You can admire it from the viewing platform above or hike down to its base.
**Practical information about Háifoss Waterfall:**
*   **Location:** Þjórsárdalur, South Iceland  
*   **Access:**Reached by a rough gravel road; check vehicle and road requirements before travelling  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Access is highly dependent on road and weather conditions  
*   **Good to know:** Check current road conditions before setting out; this isn’t a casual winter roadside stop

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
### 6. Hjálparfoss
Hjálparfoss is a smaller waterfall where two streams of the Fossá meet among lava formations before flowing into a broad pool. The name roughly translates to “Help Falls.” Why? That’s because it’s traditionally linked to travellers finding grazing land for their horses after crossing harsher Highland terrain.
**Practical information about Hjálparfoss Waterfall:**
*   **Location:**Þjórsárdalur, South Iceland  
*   **Access:** A short walk from the parking area  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Conditions permitting; check the road before travelling  
*   **Good to know:** Pair it with other Þjórsárdalur sights, like the Stöng Viking-era longhouse, for a slower day away from the main road
Waterfalls in West Iceland come in all shapes and sizes, from gentle cascades to tall falls tucked into deep valleys. Many are also easy to add to a road trip through Borgarfjörður, Hvalfjörður, or the Snæfellsnes Peninsula.

## Top Waterfalls in East Iceland
### 4. Stuðlafoss Waterfall
Stuðlafoss makes a great introduction to Stuðlagil Canyon, with water tumbling over the same columnar basalt that defines the area. You’ll find this beautiful waterfall along the eastern hiking route. From the east parking area, it’s about 2.5 km (1.6 mi ) onward to Stuðlagil. So, you can easily combine both sights in one visit.
**Practical information about Stuðlafoss Waterfall:**
*   **Location:** Near Stuðlagil Canyon, East Iceland  
*   **Access:**Reached from the eastern Stuðlagil hiking route/parking area  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Conditions permitting; trails can be snowy and slippery  
*   **Good to know:** Consider joining a guided tour in winter for an easier way to explore the area in snowy or icy conditions

## Explore Iceland’s Waterfalls
Iceland’s waterfalls vary widely in size, setting, and accessibility. Some are located just off the Ring Road, while others require a longer hike to reach. Conditions also change throughout the year, with stronger water flow common in summer and frozen sections possible in winter. With waterfalls found across the country, it’s easy to include several in almost any Iceland itinerary.

Háifoss means “High Waterfall,” and at around 122 m (400 ft), it certainly lives up to its name. The Fossá River plunges into a deep canyon in Þjórsárdalur, with neighbouring Granni adding another waterfall to the scene.
_Stranger Things_ fans might recognise this landscape, too. Háifoss and Granni made an appearance in the show’s final season, giving you one more reason to visit it. You can admire it from the viewing platform above or hike down to its base.
**Practical information about Háifoss Waterfall:**
*   **Location:** Þjórsárdalur, South Iceland  
*   **Access:**Reached by a rough gravel road; check vehicle and road requirements before travelling  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Access is highly dependent on road and weather conditions  
*   **Good to know:** Check current road conditions before setting out; this isn’t a casual winter roadside stop

## Top Waterfalls in South Iceland
### 6. Hjálparfoss
Hjálparfoss is a smaller waterfall where two streams of the Fossá meet among lava formations before flowing into a broad pool. The name roughly translates to “Help Falls.” Why? That’s because it’s traditionally linked to travellers finding grazing land for their horses after crossing harsher Highland terrain.
**Practical information about Hjálparfoss Waterfall:**
*   **Location:**Þjórsárdalur, South Iceland  
*   **Access:** A short walk from the parking area  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Conditions permitting; check the road before travelling  
*   **Good to know:** Pair it with other Þjórsárdalur sights, like the Stöng Viking-era longhouse, for a slower day away from the main road
Waterfalls in West Iceland come in all shapes and sizes, from gentle cascades to tall falls tucked into deep valleys. Many are also easy to add to a road trip through Borgarfjörður, Hvalfjörður, or the Snæfellsnes Peninsula.

Stuðlafoss makes a great introduction to Stuðlagil Canyon, with water tumbling over the same columnar basalt that defines the area. You’ll find this beautiful waterfall along the eastern hiking route. From the east parking area, it’s about 2.5 km (1.6 mi ) onward to Stuðlagil. So, you can easily combine both sights in one visit.

*   **Location:** Near Stuðlagil Canyon, East Iceland  
*   **Access:**Reached from the eastern Stuðlagil hiking route/parking area  
*   **Accessible in winter?** Conditions permitting; trails can be snowy and slippery

## Architecture and style
#### The Salons of the Sun and Moon
[edit]
At the east and west end of the Avant foyer there are the _Salon du Soleil_ (Salon of the Sun) and the _Salon de la Lune_ (Salon of the Moon). They were designed as the entrance vestibules for the smoking room and the Galerie du Glacier. Their themes were heat for the smoking room and cold for the Glacier, but because they completed in haste in order to be ready for the inauguration of 1875, in the rush there was a mistake and the themes were reversed.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Garnier#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFontaine2018220-40)
This hall, 18 metres (59 ft) high, 54 metres (177 ft) long and 13 metres (43 ft) wide, was designed to act as a drawing room for Paris society. It was restored in 2004. Its ceiling was painted by Paul-Jacques-Aimé Baudry and represents various moments in the history of music. The foyer opens onto an outside loggia and is flanked by two octagonal salons with ceilings painted by Jules-Élie Delaunay in the eastern salon and Félix-Joseph Barrias in the western salon. The octagonal salons open to the north into the Salon de la Lune at the western end of the Avant-Foyer and the Salon du Soleil at its eastern end.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Garnier#cite_note-Fontaine2004p152-41)

Title: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont Paris: Visitor Guide
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
Parc des Buttes-Chaumont is the fifth-largest park in Paris, covering 25 hectares (62 acres) in the 19th arrondissement. It is also the most topographically unusual: the landscape rises and drops by over 40 metres, producing genuine cliffs, a 50-metre rocky peak, a grotto with artificial stalactites, and a waterfall, all carved out of what was once an industrial wasteland. Most visitors arriving for the first time are surprised by how wild it feels within the city limits.
Unlike the manicured symmetry of the Jardin des Tuileries or the formal geometry of the Jardin du Luxembourg, Buttes-Chaumont was designed as a romantic English-style landscape garden, full of winding paths, sudden viewpoints, and deliberate surprises. The park is open every day of the year, free of charge, and draws an almost entirely local crowd.
ℹ️ Good to know
Opening hours vary by season: roughly 7:00 am to 8:00 pm in winter and up to 10:00 pm in summer. Verify current hours at paris.fr before visiting.

## A Place Built on Dark Ground: The History
Before Haussmann's transformation of Paris in the 1860s, this corner of the 19th arrondissement served successively as an execution ground, a gypsum quarry, a dumping site, and a carcass-rendering operation. Emperor Napoleon III commissioned its redesign to give working-class Parisians a large public green space comparable to London's parks. Baron Haussmann oversaw the project and assigned the landscape design to Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand, who was responsible for all of Paris's major Second Empire parks. Construction ran from 1864 to 1867, with workers excavating the lake by hand and constructing the cliffs from quarried stone. The park opened on April 1, 1867, timed to coincide with the Exposition Universelle.
The Temple de la Sibylle, a small circular colonnade modelled on the Temple of Vesta in Tivoli, Italy, was added in 1869 at the island's summit. At 50 metres above the lake surface, it remains the park's most recognisable feature and its highest point.

## Tickets & tours

## What You Actually See: A Walkthrough
Entering from the Buttes-Chaumont metro stop, you arrive in the lower northern section: wide lawns used for picnicking from the first warm day of spring through October, a Guignol puppet theater, and a small pony circuit. The smell in the early morning is of damp grass and cut leaves; the gardening teams start at dawn, and joggers are already completing circuits around the lake.
The artificial lake covers about 1.5 hectares at the park's center. The Belvedere Island rises from the water and is reachable by two bridges: a stone arch and a narrow iron suspension bridge that sways underfoot. From the island base, 173 steps climb the rock face to the Temple de la Sibylle, where the view takes in Montmartre and the dome of Sacré-Cœur to the northwest. Late afternoon, with western light on the temple colonnade, is when this viewpoint earns its reputation.
💡 Local tip
Wear proper walking shoes. The island's upper paths are steep and can be slippery after rain. The sandal-and-cobblestones combination that works elsewhere in Paris is a liability here.
Below the main promontory on the southern shore is the park's grotto: a low cave with artificial stalactites and a small interior waterfall, dim and cool even in summer. It is one of the details many first-time visitors miss entirely.

## How the Experience Changes Through the Day
Early mornings before 9:00 am belong to joggers and dog walkers. The paths are quiet, the light is low and angled, and the lake reflects the cliffs without mid-morning visual noise. This is the best window for photography. By midday on a sunny weekend, the lawns fill with families, groups of friends, and open bottles of wine. The park is large enough to absorb a crowd without feeling compressed.
Late afternoon brings the park's most photogenic quality: golden light on the cliff faces and the lake surface. It is also when Rosa Bonheur, the park's guinguette (open-air bar and dance venue), begins to fill. Established in 2008 and run under a government mandate from the Mairie of the 19th, it is one of the more unusual hospitality setups in Paris.

## Getting There and Moving Around
The most direct access is Buttes-Chaumont station on metro line 7bis, two minutes from the northern entrance. Botzaris (also line 7bis) serves the eastern side; Laumière on line 5 covers the northwest corner. The park has 5.5 km of roads and 2.2 km of paths.
Buttes-Chaumont sits within the Canal Saint-Martin and Belleville corridor of northeast Paris. It combines naturally with a walk along the Canal de l'Ourcq or an afternoon at Parc de la Villette to the north.
⚠️ What to skip
Bicycles, scooters, and electric vehicles are not permitted inside the park for anyone over 8 years old. Vélib' racks are available at the park entrances.

## Honest Assessment: Who This Is (and Isn't) For
Buttes-Chaumont rewards visitors who want to see Paris functioning as a living city. There is no famous collection here, no ticketed experience, and no queue. If your trip is structured entirely around landmark sightseeing, this park may feel like time that could be spent elsewhere. But if you want to understand how Parisians actually use public space: where they picnic, run, drink, and spend Saturday afternoons. The park answers that question better than anywhere else in the city.
Visitors with mobility limitations should know that the dramatic viewpoints all require significant climbing. The lakeside paths are more accessible, but the island summit is not. For a flatter, fully accessible green space, the Jardin des Plantes is the more practical alternative. Rain significantly reduces the experience: the steep paths become slick and the social energy of the lawns disappears quickly.

## Cultural Footnotes
Éric Rohmer shot sequences of his 1981 film La Femme de l'aviateur here, and Jean Gabin walked the suspension bridge in Jean Grémillon's 1937 film Gueule d'amour. Each September, the park hosts the Silhouette Short Film Festival, a week of free outdoor screenings that remain one of the quieter pleasures of the Parisian autumn calendar.
The name is often misread: 'Buttes' refers to the raised terrain; 'Chaumont' derives from the old French 'chaux mont', meaning chalk or lime hill, a direct reference to the gypsum extraction that defined the site for centuries. For context on how the park fits among Paris's other green spaces, see the guide to the best parks and gardens in Paris.

## Insider Tips
*   Rosa Bonheur, the guinguette bar in the park's northeast corner, runs on a government mandate from the Mairie of the 19th and has outdoor seating, cold drinks, and weekend dancing. Arrive before 6:00 pm in summer to secure a table.  
*   The Temple de la Sibylle faces northwest directly toward Sacré-Cœur. Come late afternoon with the sun behind you for one of Paris's better Montmartre sightlines, typically without other tourists in frame.  
*   The grotto on the southern cliff face at lake level is easy to walk past. It is the most atmospheric corner of the park and is almost always empty. Look for it beneath the main promontory.  
*   Weekday mornings before 9:00 am are the quietest the park gets. Photographers and serious picnickers use this window; the weekend crowd builds quickly after 11:00 am.  
*   The Silhouette Short Film Festival runs each September with free outdoor screenings after dark inside the park. Check dates if you are in Paris during that period.

This list of **100 things to do in Paris France** helps you decide what’s actually worth your vacation time. Paris packs iconic landmarks, world-famous museums, beautiful neighborhoods, sidewalk cafés, gardens, markets, historic churches, incredible food, and romantic views into a city that can feel overwhelming when you’re trying to plan a first trip.
You will find Paris’s must-see attractions along with museums, food, outdoor activities, nightlife, shopping, viewpoints, and easy day trips. I’ve also included the experiences that make Paris memorable, from seeing the Eiffel Tower sparkle and wandering Montmartre to cruising the Seine, eating macarons, browsing a neighborhood market, and watching the city from Sacré-Cœur.
READ **Complete France Travel Guide, What You Need to Know**

### Paris at a Glance
**Best for:** Art, history, architecture, food, shopping, and romantic city breaks
**How many days:** 4–5 days for a first trip; add another day for Versailles
**Don’t miss:** Eiffel Tower, Louvre, Notre-Dame, Montmartre, and a Seine cruise
**Best museum:** Louvre for a first trip; Musée d’Orsay for Impressionism
**Best neighborhood to wander:** Montmartre or Le Marais
**Best church:** Sainte-Chapelle for stained glass; Notre-Dame for history and architecture
**Best view:** Arc de Triomphe or Sacré-Cœur
**Best garden:** Luxembourg Gardens or Tuileries Garden
**Best evening:** Seine cruise followed by the Eiffel Tower sparkling after dark
**Best food experiences:** Croissants, macarons, crêpes, cheese, pastries, and a long café lunch
**Best shopping:** Le Marais, Boulevard Haussmann, and Saint-Germain-des-Prés
**Best day trip:** Versailles
**Getting around:** Walk and use the Métro
**Good to know:** Group attractions by neighborhood instead of crossing Paris several times a day
Climbing the Eiffel Tower is a top thing to do in Paris

## 100 Unforgettable Things to Do in Paris France
### Top 10 Things to Do in Paris France
**1.** Visit the Eiffel Tower and see it sparkle after dark
**2.** Explore the Louvre
**3.** Wander Montmartre and visit Sacré-Cœur
**4.** Visit Notre-Dame Cathedral and Sainte-Chapelle
**5.** Cruise the Seine
**6.** See Impressionist masterpieces at Musée d’Orsay
**7.** Walk the Champs-Élysées and climb the Arc de Triomphe
**8.** Explore Le Marais and the Latin Quarter
**9.** Slow down for a café, pastry, crêpe, or picnic
**10.** Take a day trip to the Palace of Versailles

## 100 Unforgettable Things to Do in Paris France
### Not to Miss Landmarks in Paris
*   Walk down the famous Champs-Élysées to Arc de Triomphe and climb to the top.  
*   See the stained glass at Sainte-Chapelle.  
*   Visit the Panthéon and wander the Latin Quarter.  
*   Climb the Eiffel Tower and take in the view.  
*   Stop by the Gothic Notre Dame Cathedral on the Île de la Cité.  
*   **Spend a morning in Montmartre,** a bohemian neighborhood, and visit the Sacré-Cœur Basilica.
Sacré-Cœur Basilica in Montmartre Paris France

## 100 Unforgettable Things to Do in Paris France
### Must Do Attractions and Activities in Paris
*   Walk across Pont Alexandre III and Pont des Arts (Love Lock Bridge).  
*   Ride Le Carrousel de la Tour Eiffel.  
*   Check out the Latin Quarter, and be sure to stop in Shakespeare and Company.  
*   Tour Paris at night and watch the Eiffel Tower twinkle.  
*   Wander the streets of Île de la Cité.  
*   Pay respect to Jim Morrison and Oscar Wilde at Père Lachaise Cemetery.

The 19th arrondissement is certainly a popular neighborhood in Paris, but why not? It has beautiful green spaces, heaps of culture, and great hangout spots. All in all, a perfect place to spend time while visiting Paris. The proverbial cherry on the green space cake? A charming hilly park, Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, in Northeastern Paris, with magnificent views of the city.
This public park is an oasis of lush greenery with a waterfall, a grotto, and a Roman-style monument. Often overlooked in favor of more popular attractions like the Jardin des Tuileries or the Jardin du Luxembourg, the Parc des Buttes Chaumont is well worth a visit for a summer picnic or a picturesque weekend stroll.

**Good to know before you go (2026):**The park has begun a major renovation to stabilize the old quarry beneath it, which will last several years. For now, the Temple de la Sibylle, its island, and the Gustave Eiffel suspension bridge are closed to visitors and are expected to remain so while the studies and construction are carried out. The happy news is that about 95 percent of the park is still open, so the rolling hills, the wide lawns, the lake, and the cafes are all yours to enjoy. I will keep this guide updated as access changes.

## A brief history of Le Parc des Buttes Chaumont
The Parc des Buttes Chaumont was constructed during the reign of Napoleon III (the site was chosen by Georges-Eugène Haussmann, Baron Haussmann, who was the Prefet of Paris at the time) and was opened to the public in 1867. It is a large park, but only the fifth-largest park in Paris. It was named after a bare hill that once stood in its place (_chauve-mont_).
While the park is beautiful and scenic today, it has gruesome beginnings. In the olden days, the plot where the park stands today was a dumping ground, a disposal area for sewage, horse carcasses, and sometimes bodies of people.
Between Canal St Martin and Buttes Chaumont was the Gibbet of Montfaucon, the main gallows used to hang criminals and display their bodies to the public in the 1800s (after the French Revolution). There is a famous poem called “Ballade des pendus” (ballad of the hanged), also known as “Épitaphe Villon” or “Frères humains” by François Villon, that speaks to this.
Before then, until the 16th century, the area was well known for its gypsum quarry and limestone quarry.
In 1860, Napoleon III decided to transform the area into a spectacular garden and thus began landscaping under the direction of the engineer and designer Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand, who had also created Bois de Boulogne and Bois de Vincennes.
Working with French horticulturist and landscape architect Jean-Pierre Barillet-Deschamps, Alphand brought English-style garden elements and typical 19th-century architecture to the garden. The park was opened just in time for the Universal Exhibition of Paris (Exposition Universelle de Paris).
Parc des Buttes Chaumont boasts magnificent century-old trees, ranging from the elegant Oriental plane to the exotic hazel trees from Byzance, the resilient Siberian elm, ginkgo biloba, and the majestic Lebanese cedar. In the spring after April 1st, you can also see beautiful cherry blossom trees.

The park is also home to the _Petite Ceinture_, the long-forgotten Napoleonic light railway line constructed in 1862. The tracks loop around the inside of Paris and were used to transport passengers and goods. The line was shut down and replaced by the Paris metro in 1934, but the tracks stand today.
This area of Buttes Chaumont is closed to the public, but for the adventurous souls out there, there is a hole in the fence that leads to the tracks and all the secrets within its tunnels.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
Parc Buttes Chaumont is a magnificent garden and gets more charming the more you explore. What makes the garden so fascinating is its 19th-century architectural feat and the sheer beauty of its elements. And to top it off, Buttes Chaumont is a park for the people.
The garden has an abundance of green grass accessible to the public. It is a great place for picnics and outdoor gatherings in the warmer months or on sunny days year-round. With dozens of water fountains, a couple of eateries, and endless opportunities to explore, jog, walk, and play, the park is worth a visit despite its somewhat off-the-beaten-path location.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
### The Lake and the Bridges
There are water features! The center of the park has an artificial lake that is home to many birds and other animals year-round. There are boat rentals as well.
The lake wraps around a hilly central island and attracts waterfowl, fish, and dozens of other wildlife species that are studied by students and researchers.
The park is home to a diverse array of birdlife, including enchanting tits, agile wagtails, melodious warblers, charming hedge sparrows, graceful waterfowl, elegant black swans, graceful geese, delightful mallards, lively black-headed gulls, and cheerful water hens. Furthermore, it boasts a thriving fish population, with gudgeon, roach, tench, and pike adding to its vibrant ecosystem.
In the spring, you can also spot some cherry blossoms and heaps of spring blooms. The park has a bunch of bridges, the best of which is a suspension bridge designed by Gustave Eiffel himself. Do note that this footbridge is in the central area, which is closed for the current renovation, so for now you can admire it from a distance rather than walk across it.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
### Temple de la Sybille
Temple de la Sybille (designed by Gabriel Davioud), based on the Temple of Vesta in Tivoli, Italy, is a Roman-style monument built on a man-made cliff. It has its own little island in the lake and is accessible via two bridges. It sits on its own little island in the lake, normally reached by two footbridges. Because the island and Temple are closed for renovation work (see the note near the top of this guide), you cannot walk out to them at the moment, but they still make a beautiful sight from the paths around the lake.
The rocky peak it stands on was created by dumping topsoil to fill the holes left by the quarry, along with dynamite and other explosives to give it its ragged shape. The temple offers gorgeous views of Montmartre and the cupolas of Sacré-Cœur.
If you are a fan of the Netflix series Lupin, then you will be interested to know that the Temple de la Sibylle was featured in a few episodes of season 2.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
### Waterfall and the Secret Grotto
The hill also has a 65-foot-tall cavern that the builders turned into a grotto. It rises out of the former quarry and remains somewhat hidden from the rest of the park. Along with artificial stalactites, shadows, and light, it has an artificial waterfall, adding to the place’s magical charm.
One thing to keep in mind for 2026: the grotto and waterfall sit right below the Temple cliff, which is the part of the park under renovation, so access to this corner may be limited while the works are underway. It is worth checking the park’s official page for the latest before you make a special trip just to see it.

## What’s in and around Buttes-Chaumont?
The Buttes Chaumont garden is a massive place in itself, but the surrounding neighborhood is also worth seeing. The 19th Arrondissement is filled with beautiful open-air hangout spots, cultural spaces, and green parks. There is something to do around every corner.

Parc des Buttes-Chaumont is the fifth-largest park in Paris, covering 25 hectares (62 acres) in the 19th arrondissement. It is also the most topographically unusual: the landscape rises and drops by over 40 metres, producing genuine cliffs, a 50-metre rocky peak, a grotto with artificial stalactites, and a waterfall, all carved out of what was once an industrial wasteland. Most visitors arriving for the first time are surprised by how wild it feels within the city limits.
Unlike the manicured symmetry of the Jardin des Tuileries or the formal geometry of the Jardin du Luxembourg, Buttes-Chaumont was designed as a romantic English-style landscape garden, full of winding paths, sudden viewpoints, and deliberate surprises. The park is open every day of the year, free of charge, and draws an almost entirely local crowd.
ℹ️ Good to know
Opening hours vary by season: roughly 7:00 am to 8:00 pm in winter and up to 10:00 pm in summer. Verify current hours at paris.fr before visiting.

## A Place Built on Dark Ground: The History
Before Haussmann's transformation of Paris in the 1860s, this corner of the 19th arrondissement served successively as an execution ground, a gypsum quarry, a dumping site, and a carcass-rendering operation. Emperor Napoleon III commissioned its redesign to give working-class Parisians a large public green space comparable to London's parks. Baron Haussmann oversaw the project and assigned the landscape design to Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand, who was responsible for all of Paris's major Second Empire parks. Construction ran from 1864 to 1867, with workers excavating the lake by hand and constructing the cliffs from quarried stone. The park opened on April 1, 1867, timed to coincide with the Exposition Universelle.
The Temple de la Sibylle, a small circular colonnade modelled on the Temple of Vesta in Tivoli, Italy, was added in 1869 at the island's summit. At 50 metres above the lake surface, it remains the park's most recognisable feature and its highest point.

## What You Actually See: A Walkthrough
Entering from the Buttes-Chaumont metro stop, you arrive in the lower northern section: wide lawns used for picnicking from the first warm day of spring through October, a Guignol puppet theater, and a small pony circuit. The smell in the early morning is of damp grass and cut leaves; the gardening teams start at dawn, and joggers are already completing circuits around the lake.
The artificial lake covers about 1.5 hectares at the park's center. The Belvedere Island rises from the water and is reachable by two bridges: a stone arch and a narrow iron suspension bridge that sways underfoot. From the island base, 173 steps climb the rock face to the Temple de la Sibylle, where the view takes in Montmartre and the dome of Sacré-Cœur to the northwest. Late afternoon, with western light on the temple colonnade, is when this viewpoint earns its reputation.
💡 Local tip
Wear proper walking shoes. The island's upper paths are steep and can be slippery after rain. The sandal-and-cobblestones combination that works elsewhere in Paris is a liability here.
Below the main promontory on the southern shore is the park's grotto: a low cave with artificial stalactites and a small interior waterfall, dim and cool even in summer. It is one of the details many first-time visitors miss entirely.

## How the Experience Changes Through the Day
Early mornings before 9:00 am belong to joggers and dog walkers. The paths are quiet, the light is low and angled, and the lake reflects the cliffs without mid-morning visual noise. This is the best window for photography. By midday on a sunny weekend, the lawns fill with families, groups of friends, and open bottles of wine. The park is large enough to absorb a crowd without feeling compressed.
Late afternoon brings the park's most photogenic quality: golden light on the cliff faces and the lake surface. It is also when Rosa Bonheur, the park's guinguette (open-air bar and dance venue), begins to fill. Established in 2008 and run under a government mandate from the Mairie of the 19th, it is one of the more unusual hospitality setups in Paris.

## Getting There and Moving Around
The most direct access is Buttes-Chaumont station on metro line 7bis, two minutes from the northern entrance. Botzaris (also line 7bis) serves the eastern side; Laumière on line 5 covers the northwest corner. The park has 5.5 km of roads and 2.2 km of paths.
Buttes-Chaumont sits within the Canal Saint-Martin and Belleville corridor of northeast Paris. It combines naturally with a walk along the Canal de l'Ourcq or an afternoon at Parc de la Villette to the north.
⚠️ What to skip
Bicycles, scooters, and electric vehicles are not permitted inside the park for anyone over 8 years old. Vélib' racks are available at the park entrances.

## Honest Assessment: Who This Is (and Isn't) For
Buttes-Chaumont rewards visitors who want to see Paris functioning as a living city. There is no famous collection here, no ticketed experience, and no queue. If your trip is structured entirely around landmark sightseeing, this park may feel like time that could be spent elsewhere. But if you want to understand how Parisians actually use public space: where they picnic, run, drink, and spend Saturday afternoons. The park answers that question better than anywhere else in the city.
Visitors with mobility limitations should know that the dramatic viewpoints all require significant climbing. The lakeside paths are more accessible, but the island summit is not. For a flatter, fully accessible green space, the Jardin des Plantes is the more practical alternative. Rain significantly reduces the experience: the steep paths become slick and the social energy of the lawns disappears quickly.
texts.7:
## Cultural Footnotes
Éric Rohmer shot sequences of his 1981 film La Femme de l'aviateur here, and Jean Gabin walked the suspension bridge in Jean Grémillon's 1937 film Gueule d'amour. Each September, the park hosts the Silhouette Short Film Festival, a week of free outdoor screenings that remain one of the quieter pleasures of the Parisian autumn calendar.
The name is often misread: 'Buttes' refers to the raised terrain; 'Chaumont' derives from the old French 'chaux mont', meaning chalk or lime hill, a direct reference to the gypsum extraction that defined the site for centuries. For context on how the park fits among Paris's other green spaces, see the guide to the best parks and gardens in Paris.

## Insider Tips
*   Rosa Bonheur, the guinguette bar in the park's northeast corner, runs on a government mandate from the Mairie of the 19th and has outdoor seating, cold drinks, and weekend dancing. Arrive before 6:00 pm in summer to secure a table.  
*   The Temple de la Sibylle faces northwest directly toward Sacré-Cœur. Come late afternoon with the sun behind you for one of Paris's better Montmartre sightlines, typically without other tourists in frame.  
*   The grotto on the southern cliff face at lake level is easy to walk past. It is the most atmospheric corner of the park and is almost always empty. Look for it beneath the main promontory.  
*   Weekday mornings before 9:00 am are the quietest the park gets. Photographers and serious picnickers use this window; the weekend crowd builds quickly after 11:00 am.  
*   The Silhouette Short Film Festival runs each September with free outdoor screenings after dark inside the park. Check dates if you are in Paris during that period.

The 19th arrondissement is certainly a popular neighborhood in Paris, but why not? It has beautiful green spaces, heaps of culture, and great hangout spots. All in all, a perfect place to spend time while visiting Paris. The proverbial cherry on the green space cake? A charming hilly park, Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, in Northeastern Paris, with magnificent views of the city.
This public park is an oasis of lush greenery with a waterfall, a grotto, and a Roman-style monument. Often overlooked in favor of more popular attractions like the Jardin des Tuileries or the Jardin du Luxembourg, the Parc des Buttes Chaumont is well worth a visit for a summer picnic or a picturesque weekend stroll.

## A brief history of Le Parc des Buttes Chaumont
The Parc des Buttes Chaumont was constructed during the reign of Napoleon III (the site was chosen by Georges-Eugène Haussmann, Baron Haussmann, who was the Prefet of Paris at the time) and was opened to the public in 1867. It is a large park, but only the fifth-largest park in Paris. It was named after a bare hill that once stood in its place (_chauve-mont_).
While the park is beautiful and scenic today, it has gruesome beginnings. In the olden days, the plot where the park stands today was a dumping ground, a disposal area for sewage, horse carcasses, and sometimes bodies of people.
Between Canal St Martin and Buttes Chaumont was the Gibbet of Montfaucon, the main gallows used to hang criminals and display their bodies to the public in the 1800s (after the French Revolution). There is a famous poem called “Ballade des pendus” (ballad of the hanged), also known as “Épitaphe Villon” or “Frères humains” by François Villon, that speaks to this.
Before then, until the 16th century, the area was well known for its gypsum quarry and limestone quarry.
In 1860, Napoleon III decided to transform the area into a spectacular garden and thus began landscaping under the direction of the engineer and designer Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand, who had also created Bois de Boulogne and Bois de Vincennes.
Working with French horticulturist and landscape architect Jean-Pierre Barillet-Deschamps, Alphand brought English-style garden elements and typical 19th-century architecture to the garden. The park was opened just in time for the Universal Exhibition of Paris (Exposition Universelle de Paris).
Parc des Buttes Chaumont boasts magnificent century-old trees, ranging from the elegant Oriental plane to the exotic hazel trees from Byzance, the resilient Siberian elm, ginkgo biloba, and the majestic Lebanese cedar. In the spring after April 1st, you can also see beautiful cherry blossom trees.

The park is also home to the _Petite Ceinture_, the long-forgotten Napoleonic light railway line constructed in 1862. The tracks loop around the inside of Paris and were used to transport passengers and goods. The line was shut down and replaced by the Paris metro in 1934, but the tracks stand today.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
Parc Buttes Chaumont is a magnificent garden and gets more charming the more you explore. What makes the garden so fascinating is its 19th-century architectural feat and the sheer beauty of its elements. And to top it off, Buttes Chaumont is a park for the people.
The garden has an abundance of green grass accessible to the public. It is a great place for picnics and outdoor gatherings in the warmer months or on sunny days year-round. With dozens of water fountains, a couple of eateries, and endless opportunities to explore, jog, walk, and play, the park is worth a visit despite its somewhat off-the-beaten-path location.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
### The Lake and the Bridges
There are water features! The center of the park has an artificial lake that is home to many birds and other animals year-round. There are boat rentals as well.
The lake wraps around a hilly central island and attracts waterfowl, fish, and dozens of other wildlife species that are studied by students and researchers.
The park is home to a diverse array of birdlife, including enchanting tits, agile wagtails, melodious warblers, charming hedge sparrows, graceful waterfowl, elegant black swans, graceful geese, delightful mallards, lively black-headed gulls, and cheerful water hens. Furthermore, it boasts a thriving fish population, with gudgeon, roach, tench, and pike adding to its vibrant ecosystem.
In the spring, you can also spot some cherry blossoms and heaps of spring blooms. The park has a bunch of bridges, the best of which is a suspension bridge designed by Gustave Eiffel himself. Do note that this footbridge is in the central area, which is closed for the current renovation, so for now you can admire it from a distance rather than walk across it.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
### Temple de la Sybille
Temple de la Sybille (designed by Gabriel Davioud), based on the Temple of Vesta in Tivoli, Italy, is a Roman-style monument built on a man-made cliff. It has its own little island in the lake and is accessible via two bridges. It sits on its own little island in the lake, normally reached by two footbridges. Because the island and Temple are closed for renovation work (see the note near the top of this guide), you cannot walk out to them at the moment, but they still make a beautiful sight from the paths around the lake.
The rocky peak it stands on was created by dumping topsoil to fill the holes left by the quarry, along with dynamite and other explosives to give it its ragged shape. The temple offers gorgeous views of Montmartre and the cupolas of Sacré-Cœur.
If you are a fan of the Netflix series Lupin, then you will be interested to know that the Temple de la Sibylle was featured in a few episodes of season 2.

## Why do people like going to Parc des Buttes-Chaumont?
### Waterfall and the Secret Grotto
The hill also has a 65-foot-tall cavern that the builders turned into a grotto. It rises out of the former quarry and remains somewhat hidden from the rest of the park. Along with artificial stalactites, shadows, and light, it has an artificial waterfall, adding to the place’s magical charm.
One thing to keep in mind for 2026: the grotto and waterfall sit right below the Temple cliff, which is the part of the park under renovation, so access to this corner may be limited while the works are underway. It is worth checking the park’s official page for the latest before you make a special trip just to see it.

## What’s in and around Buttes-Chaumont?
The Buttes Chaumont garden is a massive place in itself, but the surrounding neighborhood is also worth seeing. The 19th Arrondissement is filled with beautiful open-air hangout spots, cultural spaces, and green parks. There is something to do around every corner.
